title: The Architecture of Financial Services Law
summary: How financial services legislation is typically structured, the objectives it must serve, and how international standards and existing national law shape the drafter's task.
contentGaps: Written as part of a programme: Aim and Purpose is the module's one-line description; audience, prior knowledge and core reading come from the programme

sections.Aim and Purpose: How financial services legislation is typically structured, the objectives it must serve, and how international standards and existing national law shape the drafter's task.
Learning Objectives: Describe the typical structure of a financial services statute
Explain how statutory objectives guide regulators and courts
Identify the international standards that legislation must reflect
Syllabus: Single statutes, sectoral statutes and consolidation
Statutory objectives, principles and duties of the regulator
Translating core principles and FATF standards into national law
Interaction with company, insolvency, contract and criminal law
Intended Audience: Legislative drafters and parliamentary counsel working on financial services, payments and digital asset legislation
Legal advisers in finance ministries, central banks and other public bodies who instruct drafters or review bills
Policy officials who prepare drafting instructions and impact assessments for financial legislation
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Experience of legislative drafting or legal advice in government is helpful. No specialist knowledge of financial services is required.
Core Reading: OECD (2012), Recommendation of the Council on Regulatory Policy and Governance
OECD (2014), The Governance of Regulators, OECD Best Practice Principles for Regulatory Policy
IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation
FSB (2014), Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions
